title: Flatten the Dome, Open the Pore

scenes.tts: How does a protein turn force into ionic current? One leading model, still debated, says the answer is a shape. In purified mouse Pee-AY-zo two, curved blades bow the membrane into a dome. The dome is about twenty-eight nanometres across. Flatten it, and a pore in its centre can open.

scenes.visual: A flat membrane bows into a labelled schematic dome; a bracket marks 28 nm; the dome flattens under force arrows and the pore chip turns from closed to open.

scenes.tts: Here is the geometry. A curved cap of fixed surface area projects less area onto the plane of the membrane. The same cap, flattened, projects more. So flattening increases projected area. Anything that favours more projected area favours the flat state.
scenes.visual: The dome with a bracket below for its projected width; it flattens at fixed length and the bracket grows.
scenes.narration: Here is the geometry. A curved cap of fixed surface area projects less area onto the plane of the membrane. The same cap, flattened, projects more. So flattening increases projected area. Anything that favours more projected area favours the flat state.

scenes.tts: Now add tension in the membrane. Tension lowers the energy of a state in proportion to its larger projected area. So as tension rises, the larger-area, flat state is favoured. The energy change is minus tension times the change in projected area.

scenes.visual: Yellow tension arrows grow along the membrane, the dome flattens and the pore opens; the energy expression is shown.

scenes.tts: What is the evidence? Purified mouse Pee-AY-zo one, in artificial droplet bilayers with no other cellular components, was still activated by force. So protein plus lipid is sufficient in that preparation. In liposome vesicles, cryo E M sorted purified mouse Pee-AY-zo one into curved and flattened classes. They differ by roughly three hundred square nanometres of in-plane expansion. The authors hedge whether that is the gating transition itself.

scenes.tts: Now the arithmetic. Lewis and Grandl pressurised patches of mouse Pee-AY-zo one in a human cell line, and measured the patch radius. Take an illustrative patch, two micrometres in radius, under two thousand pascals. Tension is radius times pressure, divided by two. That gives two millinewtons per metre. Their fit has a half-activation tension of two point seven, and a slope of zero point eight. At two point zero, the fit predicts about twenty-nine percent of the plateau current.
scenes.caption: Now the arithmetic. Lewis and Grandl pressurised patches of mouse Piezo1 in a human cell line, and measured the patch radius. Take an illustrative patch, 2 micrometres in radius, under 2000 pascals. Tension is radius times pressure, divided by 2. That gives 2 mN/m. Their fit has a half-activation tension of 2.7, and a slope of 0.8. At 2.0, the fit predicts about 29 percent of the plateau current.
scenes.visual: Patch sketch with R and pressure, the tension worked out, then a Boltzmann curve with T50 marked and the 2.0 point read off at about 29 percent.

scenes.tts: Force could also arrive through protein. A tether of cadherin and actin has been proposed, from cultured cells. These two accounts are not rivals. Sufficiency in a bilayer cannot exclude a coupling route in an intact cell. A tether in cultured cells cannot abolish the lipid energetics. Keep this rule: sufficient in one preparation does not mean exclusive in another.
